```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5)
library(BayesianQDM)
```

This vignette shows the functions that help to plan a proof-of-concept
study and to explain its decision: scenarios for the operating
characteristics (`qdm_scenarios()`), the comparison of designs
(`qdm_compare()`), the search of the sample size (`qdm_find_n()`), tables of
results (`as.data.frame()`), the plot of a decision and the R code of a
design (`show_code()`). The examples use one binary endpoint, and the
functions work in the same way for the other endpoints.

```{r design}
des <- design_binary(
  n_t = 12, n_c = 12,
  prior_t = prior_beta(0.5, 0.5), prior_c = prior_beta(0.5, 0.5),
  criterion = criterion_posterior(theta_tv = 0.2, theta_mav = 0.1,
                                  gamma_go = 0.5, gamma_nogo = 0.8)
)
```

## Scenarios

`qdm_scenarios()` creates the data frame of scenarios with the columns that
the design needs (see `qdm_oc()`), and a missing or misspelled column is an
error. By default it takes all combinations of the values:

```{r scenarios}
qdm_scenarios(des, pi_t = c(0.3, 0.5), pi_c = c(0.2, 0.3))
```

The scenarios can also be given by the treatment effect `theta` and the
control group, which is convenient for two endpoints and for a
time-to-event endpoint, whose scenarios are median survival times. With
`theta = "thresholds"`, the scenarios are those that a protocol usually
reports: no effect, the minimum acceptable value (MAV) and the target value
(TV).

```{r scenarios-theta}
scen <- qdm_scenarios(des, theta = seq(0, 0.4, by = 0.1), pi_c = 0.3)
scen
qdm_oc(des, qdm_scenarios(des, theta = "thresholds", pi_c = 0.3))
```

For a continuous endpoint, `sd` gives the same standard deviation to both
groups, and `sd1`, `sd2` and `rho` do the same for two continuous
endpoints.

## Comparing designs

The design steps (see `vignette("pipe")`) accept a design, so designs that
differ in one part are made from `des`. `qdm_compare()` computes their
operating characteristics under the same scenarios, in one table with a
column that names the design:

```{r compare}
n <- c(12, 18, 24)
designs <- lapply(n, function(k) qdm_sample_size(des, n_t = k, n_c = k))
names(designs) <- paste(n, "per group")
cmp <- qdm_compare(designs, scen)
cmp
plot(cmp)
```

```{r compare-numbers, include = FALSE}
go_effect <- function(label) {
  cmp$Go[cmp$design == label & abs(cmp$theta - 0.3) < 1e-9]
}
```

With an effect of 0.3, the probability of a Go decision is
`r format(go_effect("24 per group"), digits = 2)` with 24 subjects per group,
against `r format(go_effect("12 per group"), digits = 2)` with 12 subjects per
group. Other parts of a design are compared in the same way, for example the
borrowing of external control data through a power prior:

```{r compare-borrowing}
ext <- des |>
  qdm_external(external_c = borrow(data_binary(n = 40, y = 12), a0 = 0.5))
qdm_compare(list(Concurrent = des, Borrowing = ext), scen) |>
  plot(decisions = c("Go", "NoGo"))
```

## Choosing the sample size

`qdm_find_n()` is the counterpart of `qdm_calibrate()`: with the thresholds
fixed, it finds the smallest candidate sample size for which the
probability of meeting the Go criterion when the treatment has no effect,
and that of meeting the NoGo criterion when the effect is 0.3, are both at
most 0.1:

```{r find-n}
res <- qdm_find_n(des,
                  scenario_go = data.frame(pi_t = 0.3, pi_c = 0.3),
                  scenario_nogo = data.frame(pi_t = 0.6, pi_c = 0.3),
                  target_go = 0.1, target_nogo = 0.1,
                  n_t = seq(6, 30, by = 2))
res
plot(res)
```

```{r find-n-text, include = FALSE}
stable_text <- if (is.na(res$n_t_stable)) {
  "the largest candidate does not meet them"
} else if (res$n_t_stable == res$n_t) {
  "every larger candidate also meets them"
} else {
  sprintf(paste("some larger candidates do not, and every candidate from",
                "%d subjects per group on meets them"), res$n_t_stable)
}
```

The smallest candidate that meets both targets has `r res$n_t` subjects per
group. The outcomes of a binary endpoint are discrete, so the probabilities
do not decrease steadily as the sample size increases: here
`r stable_text`. `res$design` is the design with the chosen sample size.

## Tables of results

`as.data.frame()` converts a decision, a calibration or a search of the
sample size to a data frame with one row, so that results can be combined
with `rbind()` and written to a file with `write.csv()`. For example, the
decisions for the same data with three prior distributions:

```{r tables}
priors <- list(Jeffreys = prior_beta(0.5, 0.5), Uniform = prior_beta(1, 1),
               Skeptical = prior_beta(2, 6))
decisions <- lapply(priors, function(p) {
  des |>
    qdm_prior(prior_t = p, prior_c = p) |>
    qdm_decide(data_t = data_binary(12, 8), data_c = data_binary(12, 4))
})
do.call(rbind, lapply(decisions, as.data.frame))
```

The operating characteristics of `qdm_oc()` and `qdm_compare()` are data
frames already.

## Explaining a decision

`plot()` of a decision shows how the data lead to it. For one endpoint and
a criterion based on posterior probability, it shows the posterior density
of the treatment effect with the Go and NoGo regions:

```{r plot-decision}
dec <- qdm_decide(des, data_t = data_binary(12, 8),
                  data_c = data_binary(12, 4))
plot(dec)
```

For a predictive criterion, it shows the predictive probabilities with their
thresholds, and for two endpoints the probabilities of the regions.

## R code of a design

`show_code()` writes the R code that creates a design, as a pipe of the
design steps or as a call of the `design_*()` function:

```{r code}
show_code(res$design)
show_code(res$design, style = "design")
```

`show_report(x, code = TRUE)` adds the code to the end of the report of a
design or of a result (see `vignette("pipe")`).
